chronicle: A chronicle survives in different manuscript versions. This translated edition requires comparison and contextual reading.
fulford: Modern historical synthesis; exact battlefield deployments remain uncertain.
norman: English Heritage: Hastings and the conquest
Distinguish victory in battle from the longer establishment of control.
india: National Army Museum: Captain William Leith-Ross, 57th Rifles
A documented officer and unit context corroborate deployment, not every detail of the classroom Ganga Singh narrative.
ypres: A Canadian institutional account: compare its emphasis with French and North African testimony.
algeria: French Ministry of Defence: North African soldiers, 1914–1918
Different regiments and individuals had different experiences; do not treat all North Africans as one unit.
mike: Draws on personal testimony and scholarship. Some popular accounts disagree on the date and location of his burial under rubble.
clc: Royal Logistic Corps: Chinese Labour Corps
The British corps and the French labour programme were distinct. China was not a British or French colony.
china: NZ History: China and the First World War
Government historical overview; distinguishes recruitment programmes and military control.
class: Teacher-supplied cases and revision summaries; the Ganga Singh narrative is not a surviving personal diary.

notes: All decision dialogue, local orders and numerical outcomes are educational reconstructions. Historical anchors remain fixed. Indices are not casualty counts or historical statistics.

campaigns.title: The Northern Earls
campaigns.subtitle: Edwin & Morcar · survive the conquest
campaigns.enquiry: How far did William bring a “truckload of trouble” to England?
campaigns.role: Coordinate the followers and councils of Edwin and Morcar. In pairs, one pupil speaks for each brother; roles diverge in 1071.

rounds.title: The northern muster
rounds.brief: Hardrada and Tostig threaten York. As Edwin and Morcar, you coordinate a hurried defence. Men leaving farms need feeding; information travels slowly.
rounds.fact: Edwin was Earl of Mercia and Morcar Earl of Northumbria. They faced the invaders before Harold Godwinson arrived.
rounds.question: Who threatens the north?
answers: William and Lanfranc
Harald Hardrada and Tostig
Harold Godwinson and Edwin
rounds.explain: Hardrada was the Norwegian king; Tostig was Harold Godwinson’s brother. Keep the two Harolds distinct.

choices.title: Concentrate the muster
choices.description: Gather a stronger force, taking men away from local communities.
choices.outcome: More followers arrive together, but feeding them and leaving farms strains the district.

choices.title: Scout and coordinate
choices.description: Send messengers and scouts while forming the levy.
choices.outcome: Your information improves. Scouts cannot remove uncertainty or summon Harold instantly.

choices.title: Preserve local provisions
choices.description: Keep a smaller force and protect stores.
choices.outcome: Communities retain provisions, but the available defence is weaker.

rounds.prompt: Explain how gathering an army could create problems before fighting began.
voices: Edwin’s council: Mercian followers need time to assemble.
Morcar’s council: York faces immediate pressure.

rounds.title: Fulford: hold, then withdraw
rounds.brief: The forces clash near York. Reports describe heavy English losses, including men drowned during the defeat. Make a decision about cohesion and withdrawal. The battle’s historical result is fixed.
rounds.fact: The northern earls lost at Fulford. Harold subsequently defeated Hardrada and Tostig at Stamford Bridge on 25 September. Your decision changes only a model of preparedness and disruption.
rounds.question: Which sequence is correct?
answers: Fulford → Stamford Bridge → Hastings
Hastings → Fulford → Stamford Bridge
Stamford Bridge → Hastings → Fulford
rounds.explain: Fulford: 20 September; Stamford Bridge: 25 September; Hastings: 14 October 1066.

choices.title: Maintain a reserve
choices.description: Hold some followers back to support a withdrawal.
choices.outcome: The reserve helps some groups withdraw in order. The English army still loses the battle.

choices.title: Commit every available group
choices.description: Try to sustain the line with all your followers.
choices.outcome: The line is reinforced temporarily, but exhaustion makes the eventual withdrawal harder.

choices.title: Protect the retreat route
choices.description: Prioritise messengers and access to a way out.
choices.outcome: Withdrawal is less disorganised in this model. You cannot reverse the recorded defeat.

rounds.prompt: Why does defeat at Fulford matter to the wider events of 1066?
voices: A messenger: the line is under pressure.
A local reeve: followers need a route back to their communities.
rounds.fixed: Historical anchor: defeat at Fulford. No option changes it.

rounds.title: A crown changes hands
rounds.brief: Hardrada is dead, but William has won at Hastings. English leaders face the question of accommodation. You can influence how to approach submission, not undo Hastings.
rounds.fact: Harold Godwinson died at Hastings on 14 October. Edwin and Morcar eventually submitted to William, who was crowned at Westminster on 25 December.
rounds.question: Why was Hastings not the end of the conquest?
answers: It happened after Domesday
Winning a battle did not ensure local obedience
William immediately left England forever
rounds.explain: William still needed to secure land, leaders and communities.

choices.title: Negotiate as a delegation
choices.description: Present concerns together while acknowledging William’s strength.
choices.outcome: A joint approach preserves a negotiating voice, but the king can alter the balance later.

choices.title: Submit promptly
choices.description: Seek to preserve estates through early cooperation.
choices.outcome: Immediate danger eases. Some followers question how much independence remains.

choices.title: Consult scattered supporters
choices.description: Delay the approach while hearing local leaders.
choices.outcome: You hear more concerns, but delay brings uncertainty and mistrust.

rounds.prompt: Explain why an earl might submit without welcoming all Norman changes.
voices: Edwin’s council: preserve our family’s position.
Morcar’s council: our followers expect protection.
rounds.fixed: Historical anchor: submission and William’s coronation.

rounds.title: Rebellion and castles
rounds.brief: Discontent grows as William consolidates power. You coordinate resistance, but strongholds and an advancing royal army limit your freedom.
rounds.fact: Edwin and Morcar rebelled in 1068, then submitted as William advanced. Castle building strengthened Norman control. Their later paths must not be collapsed into immediate permanent imprisonment in 1068.
rounds.question: How could castles help William?
answers: They replaced every village
They housed troops and controlled important places
They gave every English earl more land
rounds.explain: Castles combined military bases with visible authority.

choices.title: Seek a wider alliance
choices.description: Spend provisions maintaining contacts with other opponents.
choices.outcome: Connections broaden, but promises do not guarantee coordinated action.

choices.title: Protect followers, then negotiate
choices.description: Avoid concentrating exposed communities around one confrontation.
choices.outcome: Local disruption is reduced in the model. You still face William’s superior position.

choices.title: Rally quickly with existing supplies
choices.description: Demonstrate opposition before support is secure.
choices.outcome: The rising is visible but fragile. Norman movement exposes its weaknesses.

rounds.prompt: Link rebellion, castle building and the difficulty of controlling England.
voices: Edwin’s council: authority in Mercia is slipping.
Morcar’s council: allies must act together, not merely promise.
rounds.fixed: Historical anchor: the brothers submit in 1068.

rounds.title: The cost to the North
rounds.brief: Northern revolt and Danish intervention provoke William’s response. View this regional crisis from the earls’ limited position: you are not commanders of every northern rebellion.
rounds.fact: William’s Harrying of the North devastated communities and food supplies. It strengthened coercive control through severe suffering. Exact losses and the full extent of devastation are debated.
rounds.question: Which evidence best tests the human cost of control?
answers: Only the number of castles
Damage to homes, crops and communities
Only the king’s title
rounds.explain: Ask who suffered and how long the consequences lasted; royal control and welfare are different criteria.

choices.title: Organise local relief
choices.description: Use stores and contacts to help displaced households.
choices.outcome: Some support reaches households; resources are limited against widespread destruction.

choices.title: Disperse vulnerable groups
choices.description: Prioritise routes away from the worst disruption.
choices.outcome: Some people move to relative safety, but travel and loss of homes bring further hardship.

choices.title: Retain supplies for followers
choices.description: Preserve the ability of your own following to act.
choices.outcome: Your following remains more prepared, while local needs go unmet.

rounds.prompt: Was a method that increased royal control necessarily a successful change for the population?
voices: A community representative: destroyed stores cannot feed families.
A council messenger: the wider region is beyond our control.
rounds.fixed: Historical anchor: the Harrying occurs independently of your decision.

rounds.title: Two brothers, different endings
rounds.brief: The brothers flee William’s court in 1071. Their paths separate. Your final playable decision is about surviving followers and the evidence you will carry into your judgement.
rounds.fact: Edwin was killed by his own men in 1071. Morcar went to Ely, submitted and was imprisoned. The Domesday survey came later, in 1086: it is an epilogue, not something the brothers jointly created.
rounds.question: Which ending is historically accurate?
answers: Both brothers ruled England
Edwin died; Morcar’s resistance ended in imprisonment
Both completed Domesday in 1071
rounds.explain: Keep individual lives and dates separate. Neither brother receives an invented victory ending.

choices.title: Record ordinary people’s experiences
choices.description: Prioritise accounts of loss, obligations and protection.
choices.outcome: Your dossier gives communities a voice, but one locality cannot represent all England.

choices.title: Record methods of control
choices.description: Trace castles, land grants and the suppression of resistance.
choices.outcome: Your dossier explains how power worked. You must also weigh its human cost.

choices.title: Compare both perspectives
choices.description: Assemble a shorter record of control and its uneven consequences.
choices.outcome: Your account balances perspectives but needs precise evidence to avoid a vague compromise.

rounds.prompt: Use at least two events and compare an earl, a villein and a Norman follower.
voices: Edwin’s path: killed in 1071.
Morcar’s path: Ely, submission and imprisonment.
rounds.fixed: Historical anchor: Edwin’s death and Morcar’s imprisonment.

campaigns.title: Hold the Line
campaigns.subtitle: Ganga Singh case · 57th Rifles
campaigns.enquiry: Did Indian troops make a meaningful contribution to the war effort?
campaigns.role: A reconstructed section council within the 57th Rifles, following the teaching case. You are not the Maharaja of Bikaner or an army commander.

rounds.title: Reinforcements arrive
rounds.brief: Follow the classroom Ganga Singh case through a representative 57th Rifles section. Your council chooses local priorities under orders, not the strategy of the whole army.
rounds.fact: The 57th Wilde’s Rifles served in France in 1914. The classroom Ganga Singh story is a later teaching narrative, not a verified personal diary or the biography of the Maharaja of Bikaner.
rounds.question: Which scale fits this scenario?
answers: A representative section within an Indian regiment
The whole Allied army
The Bikaner Camel Corps in Egypt
rounds.explain: The class case is a soldier of the 57th Rifles. Do not confuse people sharing a name.

choices.title: Check equipment and practise
choices.description: Invest time in familiarisation before forward movement.
choices.outcome: Handling and confidence improve; movement is slower.

choices.title: Prioritise rations and clothing
choices.description: Prepare supplies for unfamiliar conditions.
choices.outcome: Comfort and endurance improve. Equipment practice remains necessary.

choices.title: Move with minimum delay
choices.description: Keep stores for later and accept a harder arrival.
choices.outcome: The section reaches its assembly area quickly but is less settled.

rounds.prompt: How can reinforcement be useful before a unit wins any ground?
voices: Section council: arrival does not mean readiness.
Supply runner: food and usable equipment must reach the men.

rounds.title: Routes under pressure
rounds.brief: Roads are crowded. Supplies and messages must reach positions near Ypres. Your route choice trades speed against disruption.
rounds.fact: Reinforcement, communications and transport connected Indian units to the wider British force. A unit’s contribution depended on more than individual bravery.
rounds.question: What makes a supply route militarily important?
answers: It replaces the need for soldiers
It keeps positions supplied and usable
It guarantees victory
rounds.explain: Explain the chain: transport → supplies → readiness → ability to hold.

choices.title: Use a protected route
choices.description: Take longer and organise carriers in smaller groups.
choices.outcome: Fewer simulated disruptions reach the section, though deliveries take time.

choices.title: Split deliveries
choices.description: Send essentials first and keep a second load behind.
choices.outcome: The position receives essentials, with some duplication of effort.

choices.title: Use the shortest route
choices.description: Save resources but accept exposure and congestion.
choices.outcome: Movement is quick when clear; interruptions create fatigue.

rounds.prompt: Explain how logistics changes the value of reinforcements.
voices: A carrier: the shortest route is not always the most reliable.
A messenger: neighbouring positions need to know our condition.

rounds.title: Hold a threatened sector
rounds.brief: Higher command orders your position held. Choose preparation and coordination, without inventing Ganga Singh’s exact spoken thoughts or movements.
rounds.fact: Indian troops helped reinforce a hard-pressed front in 1914. Holding a position could gain time for other forces. One personal story cannot prove that one man saved the war.
rounds.question: Why can holding ground be meaningful?
answers: It can deny a breakthrough and buy time
Only advances count
Every defence ends the war
rounds.explain: Military effect can be defensive and indirect.

choices.title: Coordinate with neighbours
choices.description: Allocate runners and prepare fallback messages.
choices.outcome: The line is better connected. There is still danger and pressure.

choices.title: Strengthen cover
choices.description: Spend effort on immediate protection.
choices.outcome: Cover reduces simulated disruption, while the wider sector remains contested.

choices.title: Keep all effort on observation
choices.description: Conserve stores and watch for changes.
choices.outcome: You retain supplies, but fatigue grows and cover remains weak.

rounds.prompt: Connect holding a sector to timing and the wider front.
voices: Section council: our neighbours matter as much as our own trench.
A runner: orders and ground conditions do not always match.

rounds.title: Cold, work and relief
rounds.brief: The section needs rest and maintenance. Immediate demands compete with recovery. Fatigue from earlier rounds now affects readiness.
rounds.fact: Industrial warfare relied on repeated supply, repair and relief. Weather and exhaustion affected forces from many backgrounds; experience differed between units and individuals.
rounds.question: Why rotate duties?
answers: To remove every risk
To sustain effectiveness while allowing recovery
Because supply no longer matters
rounds.explain: Rest is part of maintaining a force, not the absence of contribution.

choices.title: Rotate rest and maintenance
choices.description: Use support to cover shorter duty periods.
choices.outcome: More people recover and equipment receives attention.

choices.title: Repair first, then rest
choices.description: Accept fatigue to restore essential kit.
choices.outcome: Equipment improves quickly; tired personnel need later relief.

choices.title: Maintain the existing pattern
choices.description: Keep provisions but accept accumulating strain.
choices.outcome: Resources remain, while exhaustion reduces resilience.

rounds.prompt: How does fatigue complicate a simple story about courage?
voices: A section representative: no one can work indefinitely.
A stores clerk: damaged kit makes routine tasks harder.

rounds.title: Measure the contribution
rounds.brief: Your staff summary must explain what the Indian Corps contributed. Select the evidence to prioritise before writing your conclusion.
rounds.fact: The class sheet reports ten miles of a twenty-five-mile British sector held by the Indian Corps. That is a claim about that British sector, not forty per cent of the entire Western Front.
rounds.question: What does the sector figure measure?
answers: All of Europe
A defined British sector
Every Indian unit throughout the war
rounds.explain: Always state the geographical and numerical denominator.

choices.title: Combine scale and timing
choices.description: Use deployment alongside the pressure on the front.
choices.outcome: Your explanation links manpower with need and timing.

choices.title: Corroborate the individual story
choices.description: Compare the teaching narrative with unit context.
choices.outcome: Your account becomes more cautious and better supported.

choices.title: Use the dramatic story alone
choices.description: Conserve effort but leave its reach untested.
choices.outcome: The story is memorable, but the argument has a weak evidential base.

rounds.prompt: Distinguish a soldier’s experience, a regiment’s role and a corps-level claim.
voices: An evidence officer: numbers need a denominator.
A researcher: a later teaching story is not a contemporary diary.

rounds.title: Beyond a battlefield score
rounds.brief: The final task is to judge contribution and recognition separately. Do not let the simulation’s indices stand in for real evidence.
rounds.fact: India was under British rule. Military service took place within unequal imperial relationships. Useful service did not automatically create equality or equal remembrance.
rounds.question: Which conclusion is strongest?
answers: Discrimination proves the work had no value
Contribution and recognition must be assessed separately
A high game score proves every claim
rounds.explain: An unfairly treated group can still make a significant contribution.

choices.title: Explain a causal chain
choices.description: Link reinforcement to holding, time and wider operations.
choices.outcome: Your dossier explains military effect rather than listing suffering.

choices.title: Compare with another group
choices.description: Set this case beside labour or another combat case.
choices.outcome: Comparison shows different ways to contribute, with limits of scale.

choices.title: Identify evidence still needed
choices.description: Record a supported conclusion and a question for further research.
choices.outcome: Your qualified judgement makes uncertainty visible.

rounds.prompt: Was this a meaningful contribution? Use evidence, a mechanism and a limitation.
voices: A historian: meaningful does not have to mean decisive alone.
A pupil council: whose contribution is remembered?

campaigns.title: Under the Gas Cloud
campaigns.subtitle: Algerian tirailleurs · Ypres
campaigns.enquiry: How should Algerian troops’ contribution be judged in the context of Second Ypres?
campaigns.role: A reconstructed local council within the French 45th Division’s Algerian troops. You do not direct the entire division or neighbouring Allied armies.

rounds.title: The Ypres salient
rounds.brief: Represent a local group of Algerian tirailleurs within the French 45th Division’s sector. This is a reconstructed unit perspective, not a named soldier’s diary.
rounds.fact: French positions at Second Ypres included North African troops. The war effort linked different imperial forces; not all units, languages or experiences were identical.
rounds.question: What was Algeria’s political relationship with France?
answers: A French colonial relationship
A British Dominion
An independent Canadian province
rounds.explain: Different imperial relationships shaped service and rights.

choices.title: Clarify routes and messages
choices.description: Spend time checking neighbouring units and fallback information.
choices.outcome: Communication improves, although higher-level decisions remain outside your control.

choices.title: Improve shelter and supplies
choices.description: Prepare the local position for continued duty.
choices.outcome: The position is better sustained but remains exposed to enemy weapons.

choices.title: Maintain the existing position
choices.description: Keep stores in reserve.
choices.outcome: The group conserves resources and accepts a less prepared position.

rounds.prompt: Why does the exact unit context matter when judging a group?
voices: A liaison runner: neighbouring units have different chains of command.
A section council: we need clear routes, not just orders.

rounds.title: An unfamiliar cloud
rounds.brief: Chlorine gas reaches French positions. Effective protection is lacking. Choose how to organise warnings and movement in a crisis. This is historical analysis, not modern gas-safety advice.
rounds.fact: The German chlorine attack caused severe casualties and opened a gap in the Allied line. Withdrawal under such conditions is not evidence of cowardice.
rounds.question: What must be considered before judging the withdrawal?
answers: Only whether soldiers moved backwards
Weapon effects, protection, orders and conditions
Only a later stereotype
rounds.explain: Judge actions in their context. An unfamiliar weapon and inadequate protection constrained choices.

choices.title: Warn and organise withdrawal
choices.description: Use runners and a rally point while helping affected comrades.
choices.outcome: Some groups remain connected in the simulation. The historical gas attack still causes severe disruption.

choices.title: Prioritise contact with neighbours
choices.description: Communicate the danger and gaps in the line.
choices.outcome: Information travels, but exposure and confusion still impose severe costs.

choices.title: Try to maintain the position
choices.description: Conserve stores while attempting the existing task.
choices.outcome: Inadequate protection makes continued duty extremely costly in this model. Resolve alone cannot cancel the weapon’s effects.

rounds.prompt: Explain why this setback cannot fairly be reduced to a judgement about courage.
voices: A runner: men are struggling to understand what has reached the line.
A medical orderly: help is needed immediately.
rounds.fixed: Historical anchor: gas causes serious losses and a gap; no option creates perfect protection.

rounds.title: Reconnect the line
rounds.brief: Survivors and neighbouring troops need information, care and coordination. You do not command the Canadian or British forces responding elsewhere.
rounds.fact: Allied efforts to stabilise the front involved several forces. The failure to achieve a decisive German breakthrough cannot be credited to one unit alone.
rounds.question: Which explanation avoids overclaiming?
answers: One small group alone saved the front
Several forces and German limitations shaped the outcome
The gas had no military effect
rounds.explain: Explain a contribution without assigning every outcome to a single cause.

choices.title: Rally and relay information
choices.description: Coordinate a local assembly point and messages.
choices.outcome: The group becomes easier to support; the wider line depends on others too.

choices.title: Medical and welfare priority
choices.description: Move effort towards affected personnel.
choices.outcome: Care improves local welfare while immediate operational capacity recovers slowly.

choices.title: Reorganise with available means
choices.description: Conserve resources and accept slower recovery.
choices.outcome: Some cohesion returns, with unresolved exhaustion and care needs.

rounds.prompt: Distinguish local action from the wider battle outcome.
voices: A liaison runner: our information is one part of a larger response.
A section council: regrouping is necessary work.

rounds.title: Relief under pressure
rounds.brief: Your group faces competing needs: supplies, relief and continued duties. Earlier fatigue changes what can be sustained.
rounds.fact: Second Ypres continued beyond 22 April. Ammunition, transport, relief and medical support mattered alongside fighting.
rounds.question: What does a high casualty total establish by itself?
answers: The exact military effect of a unit
That people suffered, requiring further evidence to assess effect
That the unit was irrelevant
rounds.explain: Suffering matters, but it is not the same measure as operational effect.

choices.title: Arrange relief and resupply
choices.description: Use resources to restore capacity without abandoning care.
choices.outcome: Readiness recovers and the group is better sustained.

choices.title: Resupply first
choices.description: Restore equipment while accepting ongoing fatigue.
choices.outcome: Operational capacity rises, with a welfare cost.

choices.title: Continue with reduced means
choices.description: Preserve stores but take on greater strain.
choices.outcome: The task continues at the expense of resilience.

rounds.prompt: Explain how a unit can contribute while needing help from others.
voices: A supply runner: readiness depends on delivery.
An orderly: illness and exhaustion do not follow a neat timetable.

rounds.title: Challenge the stereotype
rounds.brief: A report labels the retreat a failure of character. Build an evidence-based response that neither romanticises nor dismisses the troops.
rounds.fact: Colonial soldiers served within unequal systems. To assess this episode fairly, compare the weapons, protection, orders and operational context.
rounds.question: Which evidence challenges a stereotype most directly?
answers: A claim about an entire people
Specific conditions and the weapon used
An invented quotation
rounds.explain: Contextual explanation is stronger than replacing one stereotype with another.

choices.title: Compare conditions and tasks
choices.description: Set the original assignment beside the effects of gas.
choices.outcome: Your report explains constraints and avoids treating retreat as a national trait.

choices.title: Corroborate across accounts
choices.description: Compare French, Canadian and North African perspectives where available.
choices.outcome: Multiple perspectives improve the account, though surviving testimony is uneven.

choices.title: Record the uncertainty
choices.description: Reject unsupported claims and state what still needs investigation.
choices.outcome: Your conclusion is cautious and makes the evidence gap clear.

rounds.prompt: Why are sacrifice, military effect and recognition different questions?
voices: An evidence officer: whose account survives?
A historian: a national label cannot explain a battlefield decision.

rounds.title: Contribution and recognition
rounds.brief: Finish the campaign by deciding what evidence deserves emphasis in public remembrance.
rounds.fact: The class enquiry asks whether empire forces made a meaningful contribution. This requires criteria such as manpower, timing, holding positions and sustaining operations, alongside recognition.
rounds.question: Which criterion is useful for “meaningful”?
answers: Only whether a group won the war alone
What its role enabled in the wider war effort
Only the number of monuments
rounds.explain: Meaningful is broader than decisive alone, and military effect differs from remembrance.

choices.title: Explain the combat role
choices.description: Connect service to a clearly defined operational task.
choices.outcome: The report has a causal argument with a defined scope.

choices.title: Compare service and treatment
choices.description: Examine how usefulness coexisted with inequality.
choices.outcome: The report separates contribution from equal rights or recognition.

choices.title: Keep a balanced evidence dossier
choices.description: Include a supported claim, counterargument and source limit.
choices.outcome: The account makes its reach and limitations explicit.

rounds.prompt: Use the Ypres case to make a qualified judgement, then compare another campaign.
voices: A historian: acknowledge suffering without making it the only measure.
A pupil council: what would a fair account include?

campaigns.title: Service & Survival
campaigns.subtitle: Mike Mountain Horse · Kainai soldier
campaigns.enquiry: What does Mike Mountain Horse’s experience reveal about contribution and recognition?
campaigns.role: A reconstructed section council following Mountain Horse’s service. Historical events are not decisions you can undo; dialogue is not his testimony.

rounds.title: A Kainai soldier enlists
rounds.brief: Follow Mike Mountain Horse’s documented service through a reconstructed section council. You are not deciding his real enlistment or speaking his private thoughts.
rounds.fact: Mike Mountain Horse of the Kainai Nation enlisted in 1916, after his brother Albert’s death following wartime gas exposure. He served in the Canadian Expeditionary Force.
rounds.question: Which description is accurate?
answers: A Kainai man serving in the Canadian Expeditionary Force
Commander of all Canadian troops
A member of the Chinese Labour Corps
rounds.explain: His Indigenous identity and Canadian service must both remain visible.

choices.title: Training and familiarisation
choices.description: Prioritise practical preparation with the section.
choices.outcome: The model section develops skills, while training remains demanding.

choices.title: Cohesion and welfare
choices.description: Make space for communication and mutual support.
choices.outcome: Trust and endurance improve; further technical preparation is needed.

choices.title: Keep resources for deployment
choices.description: Proceed with existing preparation.
choices.outcome: The section conserves supplies but carries a readiness gap.

rounds.prompt: Explain why one soldier’s story cannot represent all First Nations service.
voices: Section council: learning to work together takes time.
Historical record: identity does not disappear inside a uniform.

rounds.title: A machine-gun section
rounds.brief: Mountain Horse served in the machine-gun section of the 50th Battalion. Allocate local effort among cover, communication and the equipment needed for the task.
rounds.fact: His service included major Western Front battles. A machine-gun section depended on teamwork and supply rather than the lone-hero image.
rounds.question: Why does unit context matter?
answers: It shows how individual service connected to collective work
It proves every man did the same task
It removes the need for sources
rounds.explain: An individual story gains meaning when linked to the role and support of the unit.

choices.title: Coordinate equipment and carriers
choices.description: Check supply and movement with supporting personnel.
choices.outcome: The section can sustain its assigned role more reliably.

choices.title: Improve cover and observation
choices.description: Prepare the position and watch changing conditions.
choices.outcome: Cover improves, with fatigue from preparation.

choices.title: Hold resources in reserve
choices.description: Rely on the position and equipment already available.
choices.outcome: The immediate task continues, but strain grows.

rounds.prompt: Connect equipment, teamwork and individual contribution.
voices: A carrier: the weapon needs supplies and maintenance.
An observer: a useful position also needs cover.

rounds.title: The cost of endurance
rounds.brief: Shelling disrupts the position. Decide how a representative section responds to exhaustion and injury. The scenario does not claim a documented decision by Mountain Horse.
rounds.fact: Mountain Horse was wounded and experienced burial under rubble. Published accounts differ on precise details; the campaign does not present a disputed date or location as settled.
rounds.question: What should a historian do when accounts differ?
answers: Silently choose the most dramatic version
Compare evidence and acknowledge uncertainty
Invent an exact date
rounds.explain: Uncertainty should be visible; a vivid account is not automatically the most reliable.

choices.title: Prioritise recovery and care
choices.description: Use resources and reduce immediate demands.
choices.outcome: Welfare improves, while operational output temporarily slows.

choices.title: Rotate the work
choices.description: Share tasks to balance immediate needs with recovery.
choices.outcome: The section maintains some capacity without asking everyone to work continuously.

choices.title: Meet the task with existing personnel
choices.description: Save supplies while accepting serious strain.
choices.outcome: The task is attempted, but exhaustion reduces resilience.

rounds.prompt: How does recovery contribute to sustained service?
voices: A medical orderly: endurance has physical limits.
A source researcher: the precise date needs corroboration.

rounds.title: Return to operations
rounds.brief: Later operations demand coordination and renewed movement. Your earlier decisions affect the section’s readiness, not the recorded outcome of the war.
rounds.fact: Mountain Horse’s service included Cambrai and Amiens. His award of the Distinguished Conduct Medal records recognised bravery; it does not measure all Indigenous contributions.
rounds.question: What does a medal establish?
answers: A recognised act or record of bravery, with limits to what it represents
The experience of every First Nations soldier
That discrimination ended
rounds.explain: Recognition of an individual and the treatment of a wider community are different scales.

choices.title: Plan with neighbouring groups
choices.description: Prioritise coordination before moving.
choices.outcome: The section’s task is better connected to supporting units.

choices.title: Secure resupply and care
choices.description: Maintain the capacity to continue after movement.
choices.outcome: The section is better sustained through its next duties.

choices.title: Move with limited preparation
choices.description: Conserve supplies and accept uncertainty.
choices.outcome: The immediate task advances, with greater disruption in the model.

rounds.prompt: Explain why bravery and logistics belong in the same account.
voices: A liaison runner: an isolated success can be hard to sustain.
A section council: what happens after the first move?

rounds.title: Home, service and inequality
rounds.brief: The war is over, but service and return are different experiences. Your decision concerns the evidence to include in a return-home report.
rounds.fact: Mountain Horse returned in 1919 with the Distinguished Conduct Medal. First Nations veterans returned to continuing colonial inequalities; individual recognition did not guarantee equal treatment.
rounds.question: Which statement best separates contribution from rights?
answers: Service automatically produced equality
A soldier could contribute substantially and still face inequality
Unequal treatment makes service meaningless
rounds.explain: Do not use later injustice to erase wartime service, or service to erase injustice.

choices.title: Compare military and civilian records
choices.description: Look for changes and continuities across the return home.
choices.outcome: The report examines more than military recognition.

choices.title: Record community perspectives
choices.description: Include questions the official service record may not answer.
choices.outcome: The dossier makes room for identity and continuing inequality.

choices.title: State a supported, limited conclusion
choices.description: Avoid claims beyond the available evidence.
choices.outcome: The conclusion is narrower, but more defensible.

rounds.prompt: Did military recognition mean equal rights? Explain your distinction.
voices: An evidence officer: an award and a pension system answer different questions.
A historian: whose definition of service shapes the record?

rounds.title: The remembered war
rounds.brief: Mountain Horse’s experiences were recorded with Ambrose Two Chiefs on a painted war robe. Choose how to interpret visual remembrance beside official records.
rounds.fact: The war robe is a source shaped by cultural form, memory and selection. It can reveal what mattered to its makers; a service record answers different questions.
rounds.question: How should the robe be used?
answers: As an exact neutral photograph of every event
Alongside other sources, considering purpose and selection
Rejected because it is visual
rounds.explain: Different source forms have different strengths; neither is automatically complete.

choices.title: Compare robe and service record
choices.description: Ask what each source reveals and leaves out.
choices.outcome: Your account combines cultural memory and official documentation.

choices.title: Trace one recorded experience
choices.description: Study a selected event without generalising to every soldier.
choices.outcome: Your analysis is precise, with a clearly limited scope.

choices.title: Build a question-led dossier
choices.description: Record a claim, an uncertainty and further evidence needed.
choices.outcome: Your interpretation is transparent about its limits.

rounds.prompt: How does this source help judge meaningful contribution and remembrance?
voices: A historian: selection is evidence of meaning, not proof of uselessness.
A pupil council: what could the robe show that an official form cannot?

campaigns.title: The Supply Lifeline
campaigns.subtitle: Chinese Labour Corps
campaigns.enquiry: How could non-combat labour make a meaningful contribution to the war effort?
campaigns.role: A reconstructed British CLC work-party council. Coordinate labour, logistics and welfare. Workers do not become infantry or receive rifle-ammunition orders.

rounds.title: Recruitment and arrival
rounds.brief: Represent a British Chinese Labour Corps work party. Tasks are assigned under military control. You coordinate workload and welfare, not armed combat.
rounds.fact: British CLC workers began arriving in France in 1917. The French labour programme was separate; China was not a British or French colony.
rounds.question: Which description fits the CLC?
answers: Non-combatant labour under military control
An infantry assault division
A British colony
rounds.explain: Non-combatant describes the role; it does not mean work was safe or unimportant.

choices.title: Clarify tasks and communication
choices.description: Invest in interpreting instructions and work routines.
choices.outcome: Fewer simulated misunderstandings interrupt the work.

choices.title: Prioritise camp welfare
choices.description: Organise rest, food and basic support.
choices.outcome: The party begins with better endurance, though tasks still need training.

choices.title: Begin with existing arrangements
choices.description: Conserve supplies and accept a difficult transition.
choices.outcome: Work starts quickly; communication and fatigue remain concerns.

rounds.prompt: Why must China’s position be distinguished from India’s or Algeria’s?
voices: A work-party council: understanding the task matters.
Historical context: recruitment does not make China a colony.

rounds.title: Keep the port moving
rounds.brief: Cargo is waiting. Supplies need unloading and sorting before transport to the front. Choose a work pattern that balances throughput and fatigue.
rounds.fact: Labour at ports and depots connected ships to armies. Labour could release other personnel for combat while keeping essential materials moving.
rounds.question: How can unloading ships affect fighting elsewhere?
answers: It connects arriving supplies to operational needs
It has no military effect
It guarantees the next attack succeeds
rounds.explain: Build the indirect chain rather than equating usefulness with firing a weapon.

choices.title: Organise shifts and sorting
choices.description: Use extra support to reduce errors and allow rest.
choices.outcome: Reliable throughput improves without exhausting everyone at once.

choices.title: Prioritise essential cargo
choices.description: Move the most urgently needed loads first.
choices.outcome: Critical cargo moves, with a backlog and added strain.

choices.title: Extend the work period
choices.description: Conserve resources while asking more of the same party.
choices.outcome: More work is attempted now, but fatigue threatens later reliability.

rounds.prompt: Explain the chain from a crate on a ship to an operational army.
voices: A depot coordinator: urgency and importance are not always identical.
A work-party council: tomorrow’s capacity matters too.

rounds.title: A broken supply route
rounds.brief: A transport route needs repair. Decide how to allocate work before supplies can move reliably. The map shows relationships, not an exact historical work site.
rounds.fact: CLC work included roads and railways. Damage or delay behind the lines could affect the ability of fighting units to operate.
rounds.question: Why is rail repair a contribution?
answers: It restores a connection used by supplies and people
Only infantry work counts
It removes all supply problems
rounds.explain: The effect is indirect but can be essential.

choices.title: Repair the critical link first
choices.description: Concentrate skilled workers and tools at the bottleneck.
choices.outcome: The route is restored sooner in the model, but concentrated work is tiring.

choices.title: Use a staged repair plan
choices.description: Balance partial access, checks and rotating duties.
choices.outcome: Throughput returns gradually with less accumulated strain.

choices.title: Work with available tools
choices.description: Save resources and accept slower progress.
choices.outcome: Some repairs are completed, while delays persist.

rounds.prompt: What would happen to the front if this link remained unusable?
voices: A transport coordinator: a small bottleneck can delay a large flow.
A work-party council: tools and recovery affect speed.

rounds.title: The repair workshop
rounds.brief: Skilled workers are needed for equipment maintenance. Choose how to balance the urgent workload with checks and recovery. This is not a claim that every labourer repaired tanks.
rounds.fact: Some Chinese workers undertook skilled repair, including work on vehicles and tanks. The class case connects repair and railway work to operational preparation.
rounds.question: Which claim is appropriately precise?
answers: Every Chinese worker was a tank mechanic
Some skilled workers helped maintain equipment
The CLC commanded tank assaults
rounds.explain: Distinguish different workers and tasks within a large labour force.

choices.title: Pair skilled workers and learners
choices.description: Invest in checks and shared skills.
choices.outcome: The workshop develops more reliable capacity, with time spent training.

choices.title: Triage urgent repairs
choices.description: Prioritise equipment most needed for current operations.
choices.outcome: Priority repairs move faster while other work waits.

choices.title: Maintain the existing workload
choices.description: Conserve resources despite a growing queue.
choices.outcome: Some equipment returns to use, but fatigue and backlog grow.

rounds.prompt: Explain why repairs can matter even when a worker never enters a tank in battle.
voices: A workshop coordinator: returning equipment to use is a military effect.
A work-party council: more hours are not always more reliable work.

rounds.title: The war’s dangerous aftermath
rounds.brief: The Armistice has stopped the fighting, but work continues. The party faces damaged ground and dangerous remains. Choose organisational priorities; no option teaches clearance techniques.
rounds.fact: Chinese workers remained for postwar tasks including battlefield clearance and reconstruction. The Armistice did not immediately end their service or the danger.
rounds.question: What changed after the Armistice?
answers: All danger and work ended immediately
The tasks changed, but dangerous work continued
CLC workers became assault infantry
rounds.explain: War’s effects outlast the formal fighting.

choices.title: Checks, reporting and rotation
choices.description: Use support for oversight, communication and shorter duty periods.
choices.outcome: The work proceeds more cautiously; risk cannot be eliminated.

choices.title: Prioritise essential reconstruction
choices.description: Focus effort on routes and places needed for recovery.
choices.outcome: Restoration progresses, while demands and hazards remain.

choices.title: Work with limited additional support
choices.description: Save resources while accepting slower and harder work.
choices.outcome: Some work is completed, but fatigue and welfare pressures grow.

rounds.prompt: Why should the campaign continue beyond 11 November 1918?
voices: A work-party council: peace does not restore a landscape overnight.
A reconstruction coordinator: work and risk continue.

rounds.title: An essential contribution
rounds.brief: The final British CLC workers returned in 1920. Judge the military and postwar significance of their work, alongside treatment and recognition.
rounds.fact: Nearly 100,000 workers served in the British corps by 1918; the familiar total of around 140,000 refers to Chinese workers supporting Britain and France together. The final British CLC return was in September 1920.
rounds.question: What does the total around 140,000 refer to?
answers: Only British infantry
Workers for Britain and France combined
Only tank mechanics at one workshop
rounds.explain: Totals from different programmes must not be merged into one unit.

choices.title: Trace logistical effects
choices.description: Connect work to transport, equipment and operations.
choices.outcome: Your dossier explains why labour could be meaningful without combat.

choices.title: Compare contribution and recognition
choices.description: Assess usefulness separately from segregation or neglect.
choices.outcome: Your account links military value with unequal experience.

choices.title: Record a qualified conclusion
choices.description: State what the evidence establishes and what it cannot.
choices.outcome: Your judgement is supported without treating a large total as sufficient proof.

rounds.prompt: Compare this non-combat contribution with a combat campaign using the same criteria.
voices: A historian: essential labour can disappear from a battle-centred account.
A pupil council: whose work made operations possible?
